Yes — very likely.

At 18:03 EET in Cairo, the Moon is about **37° above the horizon** in the southwest (**azimuth ~217°**), which is a comfortably high, unobstructed position. It is a **~26% illuminated crescent**, so it is not especially bright, but it should still be readily visible to normal unaided eyesight under a clear sky.

The main limiting factor is the **astronomical twilight**: the Sun is only about **13.5° below the horizon**, so the sky is not fully dark yet, especially toward the western/southwestern part of the sky. But the Moon is roughly **61° from the Sun**, a substantial separation, and its altitude places it well above the brightest near-horizon twilight glow.

My honest estimate: **you should be able to spot it without optical aid**, probably as a fairly obvious crescent once you look in the right southwest area. It may not “pop” as dramatically as it would later in full darkness, and haze, city light pollution, or nearby buildings could make it less conspicuous, but with a clear view of the southwest sky I’d expect a good chance—roughly **80–95%**.
